newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower at long end, 3-mo stronger.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower at long end, 3-mo stronger.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities closed sharply lower at the long end of the maturity spectrum on Wednesday as hedge fund selling and supply worries weighed on the market.
Concerning market participants was a sharp drop in the March U.S. trade gap -- a 19.3 percent fall to $8.51 billion -- a strong indication that the economy continued to grow.
However, the short end of the market continued to prosper, as expected, after the Federal Reserve's policy-making arm voted to leave monetary policy unchanged on Tuesday.

The Treasury Department said on Wednesday that it had posted a record budget surplus of $93.94 billion in April, up from its $72.40 billion surplus in the same period last year. Surpluses usually are high in April due to tax payments and often force the Fed to add reserves to the banking system on a temporary basis or permanently via coupon or bill passes.

"There was strong selling for a couple of hours in the morning and some rumors of hedge funds selling futures," said Christopher Rupkey, financial economist at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi. "But it was technical day for the most part."

"You can talk all you want about the Fed being behind the curve, but we've seen no further advancement behind what should be good news" with the Fed voting to leave monetary policy unchanged, Rupkey said.
That had all the hallmarks of a very weak bond market, he said. The market still was not rising despite a budget accord being reached last week, he said.
"It seems it can't go up, and that's why maybe we saw hedge fund selling," Rupkey said. The bond market should have responded more strongly to lack of action on Tuesday by the Federal Reserve.
"At these levels it's light out. We could see a one-third retracement of the recent rally seen," he said.
Rupkey said it was hard to say why the Fed paused, but politics could have played a role. They also had the leeway to tighten more gradually than in the last tightening cycle in 1994.
"If they don't do it on July 2, then we have to come up with another explanation," he said.
Debt futures ended at a two-week low after a dealer was said to have sold 10,000 contracts early in the trading session, prompting other sales, traders said.
"There were reports of hedge fund selling and unwinding of curve flattening with the Fed doing nothing," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Moran said the market didn't react strongly to trade data or the budget surplus.

Trading volume was strong, approaching $98 billion by 1600 EDT/2000 GMT, according to GovPX with volume in on-the-run coupons 62 percent above average. Volume was heaviest again in two-year securities, at about $9.5 billion.

The 30-year bond was down 24/32 at 95-24 to yield 6.96 percent. The 10-year note closed at 99-7/32, down 13/32 to yield 6.73 percent. Five-year notes ended at 100-9/32, down 6/32 to yield 6.56 percent.
Near the shorter end of the maturity range, two-year notes closed at 99-9/32, off 1/32 to yield 6.22 percent.
Three-month bill rates fell eight basis points to 4.99 percent. Six-month bill rates fell two basis points to 5.24 percent. Year bill rates were unchanged at 5.47 percent.
